'''Alan Belmont Cobham''' (4 November 1927{{spaced ndash}}28 June 2011){{r|shallit}} was an American [[mathematician]] and [[computer scientist]] known for (with [[Jack Edmonds]] and [[Michael O. Rabin]]) inventing the concept of [[polynomial time]] and the [[P (complexity)|complexity class P]],{{r|kozen}}{{ran|B}} for [[Cobham's thesis]] stating that the problems that have practically usable computer solutions are characterized by having polynomial time,{{r|ausiello}}{{ran|B}} and for [[Cobham's theorem]] on the sets of numbers that can be recognized by [[finite automaton|finite automata]].{{r|durand-rigo}}{{ran|C}} He also did foundational work on [[automatic sequence]]s,{{r|rowland}}{{ran|D}} invented [[priority queue]]s and studied them from the point of view of [[queueing theory]],{{r|miller}}{{ran|A}} and wrote a program for playing [[contract bridge]] that was one of the best in the world during the mid-1980s.{{r|truscott}}

Cobham was a student at [[Oberlin College]], the [[University of Chicago]], the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], but did not complete a doctorate. He became an [[operations research]]er for the [[United States Navy]], a researcher for [[IBM Research]] at the [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]], and a professor and founding department chair of the computer science department at [[Wesleyan University]].{{r|shallit}}
